KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong/long duration Nor'easter will continue to 
bring damaging wind gusts, coastal flooding/beach erosion, and 
periods of heavy rain through the weekend. Rain and gusty winds 
persist into  Monday. 

Impacts from this Nor’easter are well underway, with satellite 
imagery showing a distinct, rotating low-pressure center positioned 
just to our south. Evident bands of higher cloud tops indicate 
robust convection, which is being reflected on radar as convective 
showers and even a few embedded thunderstorms. This afternoon, these 
bands have pivoted into the South Coast and southeast MA. Expect 
these conditions to persist through the evening, bringing periods of 
moderate to heavy rainfall rates. Given the banded and scattered 
nature of the convection, impacts will be localized, but areas 
across southern MA, RI, and CT face the highest risk through 
tonight. While we will continue to monitor for isolated flash 
flooding under the heaviest downpours, the primary hydro threats 
remain urban ponding and poor-drainage flooding. Strong NE winds 
persist into tonight. Peak gusts of 45–60 mph were observed along 
the coast early this morning, with localized gusts of 60–70 mph 
across Block Island and the Cape and Islands. Expect 45–55 mph 
gusts, occasionally up to 60 mph to continue this afternoon, highest 
along the immediate coast.

Strong to Damaging Wind Gusts: 

Tonight, the low is forecast to slowly track northward, but west of 
the 40/70 benchmark before taking a sharp westward turn toward the 
NJ coast. As the low pivots, a potent 925mb low-level jet (LLJ) 
oriented SW-NE across southern New England will strengthen to 60–70 
kts. This introduces a renewed risk for a period of consistently 
stronger surface gusts, particularly across the South Coast, Block 
Island, and portions of CT if these winds can efficiently mix down. 
Gusts of 45–60 mph are possible in these areas, and isolated higher 
gusts along the immediate coast cannot be ruled out. As the low 
shifts further west toward NJ on Sunday, the 925mb LLJ will weaken. 
In response, winds will veer to the E/ENE, with surface gusts 
decreasing into the 30–45 mph range. The pressure gradient and 
associated jet will continue to gradually weaken as the low 
eventually loops back to the northeast and pushes offshore. Winds 
will follow suit, with gusts finally dropping below 30 mph by Monday 
night.

Prolonged Period of Steady Rain, Heavy at Times:

Abundant moisture, optimal dynamics, and marginal instability will 
maintain widespread rain impacts through the remainder of this 
event. Added low-level convergence along the higher terrain of the 
Worcester Hills and Berkshires will continue to support periods of 
moderate to heavy rain. High-resolution and global guidance 
highlights a broad footprint of 2–4” of rain, with localized 
maximums of 5–6” possible before the system and rain exit late 
Monday. Notably, the 48-hour HREF Probability Matched Mean (PMM) 
highlights areas of Rhode Island and eastern Massachusetts for 
potential 5–7” totals. Because this is primarily a prolonged 
rainfall event rather than a widespread torrential downpour, the 
overall flash flood threat is somewhat limited by the lack of 
widespread extreme rain rates. However, the sheer volume of water 
raises significant concerns for urban and poor-drainage flooding, as 
well as rapid rises on small rivers and streams. To address this 
threat, a Flood Watch has been issued for Rhode Island and eastern 
Massachusetts, aligning with the highest-confidence footprint for 
the 5–7” storm totals.

Coastal Flooding: 

The prolonged period of strong northeast winds and high offshore 
seas will continue to result in beach erosion and coastal flooding 
over multiple high tide cycles through Sunday. Storm surge values of 
1 to 2 feet, perhaps briefly approaching 2.5 feet, are expected 
along east-facing, ocean-exposed shorelines. Coastal Flood Warnings 
remain in effect along the eastern Massachusetts coast, including 
the Cape and Islands, through the Sunday night high tide cycle. 
Consideration is being given to extending these headlines into the 
Monday morning high tide cycle.

The combination of elevated water levels and 15 to 25 foot offshore 
seas will result in minor coastal flooding, with a few pockets of 
low-end moderate flooding possible during each high tide cycle. 
However, the most significant impact from this long-duration event 
is expected to be severe beach erosion given the persistent strong 
northeast winds and large waves. Astronomical tides peak this 
weekend, so coastal impacts will remain a concern even as winds 
gradually diminish. In addition, water may struggle to fully drain 
between successive high tide cycles, while heavy rainfall could 
further exacerbate drainage and flooding issues.
